back: A question you can answer by measuring something, e.g. "How does ramp height affect how far a car rolls?"
A testable prediction with a reason: "If… then… because…".
The variable you change on purpose.
The variable you measure. Its value depends on the independent variable.
Variables you keep the same, so the test is fair.
Only the independent variable changes; all other variables are kept the same.

front: How do you calculate the **mean** of repeated results?
back: Add the results and divide by how many there are. Leave out any outliers.
A result that doesn't fit the pattern (an anomalous result). Check or repeat it, and leave it out of the mean.

front: Which variable goes on which axis?
back: Independent variable on the x-axis (across); dependent variable on the y-axis (up).
Line graph when both variables are numbers; bar graph when the independent variable is categories.

front: Where do units go in a results table?
back: In the column headings, e.g. "Time (s)", not after every number.
Repeating the test gives similar results. Doing repeats and taking a mean makes results more reliable.
The pattern (trend), data from your results as evidence, and whether your hypothesis was supported.

front: Common **source of error** when timing with a stopwatch
back: Human reaction time when starting and stopping it. Repeat and average, or time a longer event.

front: Why do science ideas change over time?
back: Scientists test ideas against evidence. When new evidence is found, ideas can be changed or replaced, e.g. continental drift → plate tectonics.

front: How do scientists check each other's work?
back: They share methods and results (e.g. in journals) so others can check them and repeat the experiments.
